claim: Conserved proteins drive clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME), which from yeast to humans involves a burst of actin assembly.
source: Conserved proteins drive clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME), which from yeast to humans involves a burst of actin assembly.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about CME being conserved across species and involving actin assembly.

claim: Membrane invagination speed in S. pombe is two-fold greater than in S. cerevisiae.
source: Though endocytic protein abundance in S. pombe and S. cerevisiae is more similar than previously thought, membrane invagination speed and depth are two-fold greater in fission yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 4F showing invagination speeds.

claim: Membrane invagination depth in S. pombe is two-fold greater than in S. cerevisiae.
source: Though endocytic protein abundance in S. pombe and S. cerevisiae is more similar than previously thought, membrane invagination speed and depth are two-fold greater in fission yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live-cell imaging and STORM microscopy presented in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: Accumulation of ~70 WASp molecules activates the Arp2/3 complex to drive membrane invagination in both S. pombe and S. cerevisiae.
source: In both yeasts, accumulation of ~70 WASp molecules activates the Arp2/3 complex to drive membrane invagination.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 7 and related analyses.

claim: WASp-mediated actin nucleation plays an essential role in fission yeast endocytosis.
source: In contrast to budding yeast, WASp-mediated actin nucleation plays an essential role in fission yeast endocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments with WASp CA domain deletion mutants shown in Figure 8.

claim: The assembly of two zones of actin filaments is specific for fission yeast and not essential for CME.
source: Although the assembly of two zones of actin filaments is specific for fission yeast and not essential for CME.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments with NPF mutants and live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 8.

claim: CME takes up nutrients, regulates responses to extracellular stimuli, and controls the chemical composition and surface area of the plasma membrane.
source: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) takes up nutrients, regulates responses to extracellular stimuli, and controls the chemical composition and surface area of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the functions of CME.

claim: Cells recruit several dozen highly conserved proteins to CME sites in a regular, predictable order from yeast to humans.
source: From yeast to humans, cells recruit several dozen highly conserved proteins to CME sites in a regular, predictable order to facilitate plasma membrane internalization (Engqvist-Goldstein and Drubin, 2003; Haucke and Kozlov, 2018; Kaksonen and Roux, 2018; McMahon and Boucrot, 2011; Mettlen et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Both budding and fission yeast have high internal turgor pressure, which strongly opposes plasma membrane invagination necessary for endocytosis.
source: Both budding and fission yeast have high internal turgor pressure, which strongly opposes plasma membrane invagination necessary for endocytosis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast cell biology.

claim: Actin filament assembly mediated by the Arp2/3 complex generates force to overcome plasma membrane tension in animal cells.
source: Actin filament assembly mediated by the Arp2/3 (actin-related protein 2/3) complex generates force to overcome plasma membrane tension in animal cells (Boulant et al., 2011; Merrifield et al., 2004; Merrifield et al., 2002; Yarar et al., 2005) and turgor pressure in yeast (Aghamohammadzadeh and Ayscough, 2009; Basu et al., 2014; Kaksonen et al., 2003; Sirotkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Actin filament assembly mediated by the Arp2/3 complex generates force to overcome turgor pressure in yeast.
source: Actin filament assembly mediated by the Arp2/3 (actin-related protein 2/3) complex generates force to overcome plasma membrane tension in animal cells (Boulant et al., 2011; Merrifield et al., 2004; Merrifield et al., 2002; Yarar et al., 2005) and turgor pressure in yeast (Aghamohammadzadeh and Ayscough, 2009; Basu et al., 2014; Kaksonen et al., 2003; Sirotkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The ancestors of budding yeast and fission yeast separated about 330–420 million years ago.
source: The ancestors of budding yeast and fission yeast separated about 330–420 million years ago, so these two yeasts are almost as distant from each other as either is to animal cells (Hedges, 2002; Sipiczki, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous evolutionary studies.

claim: Budding yeast and fission yeast are almost as distant from each other as either is to animal cells.
source: The ancestors of budding yeast and fission yeast separated about 330–420 million years ago, so these two yeasts are almost as distant from each other as either is to animal cells (Hedges, 2002; Sipiczki, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous evolutionary studies and represents an inference from evolutionary distance data.

claim: Actin assembly accompanies CME from yeast to humans.
source: Since actin assembly accompanies CME from yeast to humans, this association must be ancient.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the conservation of actin assembly in CME.

claim: The association between actin assembly and CME must be ancient.
source: Since actin assembly accompanies CME from yeast to humans, this association must be ancient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of actin assembly in CME across species.

claim: Lower numbers of homologous proteins were reported to be present at budding yeast endocytic sites compared to fission yeast.
source: Lower numbers of homologous proteins were reported to be present at budding yeast endocytic sites (Picco et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and some differences were reported even for the same protein in the same yeast species (Table 1) (Basu and Chang, 2011; Chen and Pollard, 2013; Epstein et al., 2018; Galletta et al., 2012; Picco et al., 2015; Sirotkin et al., 2010), highlighting the importance of direct comparisons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dynamics of WASp were reported to be distinctly different in budding and fission yeast.
source: Furthermore, the dynamics of some of the proteins including WASp, one of the main nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) for the Arp2/3 complex, were reported to be distinctly different in budding and fission yeast (Kaksonen et al., 2003; Sirotkin et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The maximum amount of spPan1 is approximately 1.7 times that of scPan1.
source: The maximum amount of spPan1 is approximately 1.7 times that of scPan1, while spEnd4 and scSla2 are present at endocytic sites in similar numbers (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: spEnd4 and scSla2 are present at endocytic sites in similar numbers.
source: The maximum amount of spPan1 is approximately 1.7 times that of scPan1, while spEnd4 and scSla2 are present at endocytic sites in similar numbers (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The maximum levels of spWsp1 are modestly higher (1.4 fold) at endocytic sites than scLas17.
source: The maximum levels of spWsp1 and spVrp1 are modestly higher (1.4 and 1.2 fold, respectively) at endocytic sites than scLas17 and scVrp1 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The maximum levels of spVrp1 are modestly higher (1.2 fold) at endocytic sites than scVrp1.
source: The maximum levels of spWsp1 and spVrp1 are modestly higher (1.4 and 1.2 fold, respectively) at endocytic sites than scLas17 and scVrp1 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The combined number of scMyo3 and scMyo5 molecules is ~1.8 times the number of spMyo1 molecules at endocytic sites.
source: The combined number of scMyo3 and scMyo5 molecules is ~1.8 times the number of spMyo1 molecules at endocytic sites (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The numbers of spArc5 and scArc15 molecules recruited to endocytic sites are indistinguishable.
source: The numbers of spArc5 and scArc15 molecules recruited to endocytic sites are indistinguishable (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The actin filament crosslinking protein spFim1 is ~1.2 fold more abundant in fission yeast than the homologous budding yeast protein, scSac6.
source: The actin filament crosslinking protein spFim1 is ~1.2 fold more abundant in fission yeast than the homologous budding yeast protein, scSac6 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: A new extracellular standard particle with 120 copies of GFP was used to calculate the absolute numbers of endocytic proteins at endocytic sites.
source: A new extracellular standard particle with 120 copies of GFP (Hsia et al., 2016) was used to calculate the absolute numbers of some of these proteins at endocytic sites and to compare the relative abundance of multiple endocytic proteins.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to the source of the nanocage standard.

claim: The mean maximum numbers at endocytic sites are 168 ± 48 molecules of Sla1.
source: Ratiometric comparisons of fluorescence intensity indicate that the mean maximum numbers (± SD) at endocytic sites are 168 ± 48 molecules of Sla1, 199 ± 72 of Myo5 and 102 ± 30 of Las17 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data using the 120-sfGFP nanocage standard presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The mean maximum numbers at endocytic sites are 199 ± 72 molecules of Myo5.
source: Ratiometric comparisons of fluorescence intensity indicate that the mean maximum numbers (± SD) at endocytic sites are 168 ± 48 molecules of Sla1, 199 ± 72 of Myo5 and 102 ± 30 of Las17 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data using the 120-sfGFP nanocage standard presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The mean maximum numbers at endocytic sites are 102 ± 30 molecules of Las17.
source: Ratiometric comparisons of fluorescence intensity indicate that the mean maximum numbers (± SD) at endocytic sites are 168 ± 48 molecules of Sla1, 199 ± 72 of Myo5 and 102 ± 30 of Las17 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data using the 120-sfGFP nanocage standard presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The 16-kinetochore clusters present in living anaphase yeast cells contain 92 ± 19 Cse4-sfGFP molecules.
source: Our measurements indicated that the 16-kinetochore clusters present in living anaphase yeast cells contain 92 ± 19 Cse4-sfGFP molecules (Figure 2D), similar to ~80 to~120 molecules counted previously using other calibration methods (Galletta et al., 2012; Lawrimore et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence microscopy data using the 120-sfGFP nanocage standard presented in Figure 2D, and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The scAbp1-GFP moves about 125 nm with relatively high regularity as the intensity approaches the maximum.
source: The scAbp1-GFP moves about 125 nm with relatively high regularity (as indicated by the small standard deviations; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) as the intensity approaches the maximum (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The transition to irregular movement of scAbp1-GFP beyond ~125 nm from the origin likely represents endocytic vesicle release in budding yeast.
source: Considering the fluorescence and EM data that reflects on endocytic membrane morphology, we conclude that the transition to irregular movement of scAbp1-GFP beyond ~125 nm from the origin likely represents endocytic vesicle release in budding yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on combining live-cell imaging data with previous EM studies.

claim: The irregular movement of spFim1-mEGFP occurs after its initial regular displacement reaches ~200 nm.
source: Strikingly, however, the irregular movement of spFim1-mEGFP (indicated by a sharp increase in the standard deviation, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) occurs after its initial regular displacement reaches ~200 nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Endocytic membrane invaginations in fission yeast appear to be substantially deeper than in budding yeast before vesicle scission occurs.
source: Since the irregular movement likely reflects diffusive movement of the free vesicle, endocytic membrane invaginations in fission yeast appear to be substantially deeper than in budding yeast before vesicle scission occurs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the particle tracking data showing different displacement distances before irregular movement.

claim: In both yeasts, the predicted scission time point is tightly correlated with the maximum intensity of the endocytic actin network.
source: Moreover, in both yeasts, the predicted scission time point is tightly correlated with the maximum intensity of the endocytic actin network (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Endocytic vesicle scission likely occurs around 4–5 s after the initiation of endocytic membrane invagination in both yeasts.
source: Thus, we conclude that endocytic vesicle scission likely occurs around 4–5 s after the initiation of endocytic membrane invagination in both yeasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of coat protein dynamics presented in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The scSla1-GFP patches in budding yeast move ~100 nm before vesicle scission.
source: The scSla1-GFP patches in budding yeast move ~100 nm before vesicle scission (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 4C.

claim: In fission yeast, spPan1-mEGFP and spSla2-mEGFP move ~200 nm during the 4–5 s after the initiation of coat protein movement and before the transition to the irregular movement phase.
source: However, in fission yeast, spPan1-mEGFP (Figure 4D) and spSla2-mEGFP (data not shown) move ~200 nm during the 4–5 s after the initiation of coat protein movement and before the transition to the irregular movement phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 4D.

claim: The fission yeast endocytic membrane invagination reaches to ~200 nm prior to vesicle scission.
source: These results suggest that that the fission yeast endocytic membrane invagination reaches to ~200 nm prior to vesicle scission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coat protein tracking data.

claim: The initiation of both spPan1-mEGFP and scSla1-GFP patch movement is tightly correlated with attainment of the maximum intensity for each protein.
source: While the initiation of both spPan1-mEGFP and scSla1-GFP patch movement is tightly correlated with attainment of the maximum intensity for each protein (Figure 4E), the invagination speed in fission yeast is about twice as fast as in budding yeast (51.8 nm/s vs 23.8 nm/s) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 4E.

claim: The invagination speed in fission yeast is about twice as fast as in budding yeast (51.8 nm/s vs 23.8 nm/s).
source: While the initiation of both spPan1-mEGFP and scSla1-GFP patch movement is tightly correlated with attainment of the maximum intensity for each protein (Figure 4E), the invagination speed in fission yeast is about twice as fast as in budding yeast (51.8 nm/s vs 23.8 nm/s) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of coat protein movement presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Actin assembly begins when spPan1-mEGFP reaches its peak intensity.
source: Actin assembly (imaged using spFim1-mCherry) begins when spPan1-mEGFP reaches its peak intensity (Figure 5B, dotted line 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The actin network begins to assemble slightly before initiation of endocytic membrane invagination.
source: These results indicate that the actin network begins to asssemble slightly before initiation of endocytic membrane invagination, and that assembly peaks around the time when scission occurs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the two-color imaging data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Actin assembly peaks around the time when scission occurs.
source: These results indicate that the actin network begins to asssemble slightly before initiation of endocytic membrane invagination, and that assembly peaks around the time when scission occurs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the two-color imaging data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The length of the spFim1 structures ranged from 120 nm to 350 nm.
source: The length of the spFim1 structures ranged from 120 nm to 350 nm (Figure 6A), which likely represents progression through the endocytic pathway (Arasada et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D-STORM imaging data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The length of spPan1 structures in fission yeast ranged from 50 nm to 180 nm.
source: The length of spPan1 structures in fission yeast ranged from 50 nm to 180 nm (Figure 6B), which is much smaller than the range for spFim1 structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D-STORM imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: spPan1 forms a ring structure in the X-Y plane, presumably encircling the invaginated membrane.
source: In addition, 3D-STORM analysis revealed that spPan1 forms a ring structure in the X-Y plane, presumably encircling the invaginated membrane (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D-STORM imaging data presented in Figure 6C, with the interpretation being speculative.

claim: The average longest axis of endocytic vesicles was 193 ± 37 nm when labeled by spFim1.
source: The average longest axis of endocytic vesicles was 193 ± 37 nm when labeled by spFim1 and 152 ± 30 nm for spPan1.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D-STORM imaging data of presumed vesicles presented in Figure 6D.

claim: The average longest axis of endocytic vesicles was 152 ± 30 nm when labeled by spPan1.
source: The average longest axis of endocytic vesicles was 193 ± 37 nm when labeled by spFim1 and 152 ± 30 nm for spPan1.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D-STORM imaging data of presumed vesicles presented in Figure 6D.

claim: mEGFP-spWsp1 only begins to move when it accumulates to its maximum level.
source: Intriguingly, our newly developed alignment software revealed that mEGFP-spWsp1 only begins to move when it accumulates to its maximum level (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 7A.

claim: mEGFP-spWsp1 patches move ~200 nm over ~4 s, while their fluorescence intensity rapidly declines to the baseline level.
source: mEGFP-spWsp1 patches then move ~200 nm over ~4 s, while their fluorescence intensity rapidly declines to the baseline level (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by particle tracking data from live-cell imaging presented in Figure 7A.

claim: spMyo1 stays non-motile during its lifetime while the actin network moves into the cytoplasm.
source: However, as in budding yeast (Sun et al., 2006), spMyo1 stays non-motile during its lifetime while the actin network moves into the cytoplasm (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Actin assembly is initiated when both spWsp1 and spMyo1 reach approximately 50% of their peak levels in fission yeast.
source: We conclude that actin assembly is initiated when both spWsp1 and spMyo1 reach approximately 50% of their peak levels in fission yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the two-color imaging data presented in Figure 7C and E.

claim: spWsp1 and spMyo1 are recruited to their maximum levels before the membrane detectably begins to invaginate.
source: Importantly, spWsp1 and spMyo1 are recruited to their maximum levels before the membrane detectably begins to invaginate, supporting the conclusion that spWsp1 and spMyo1 both promote actin nucleation to initiate membrane deformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the two-color imaging data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The rapid disassembly of spWsp1 and spMyo1 from endocytic sites supports the notion that actin nucleation by the two NPFs rapidly decreases while the invagination elongates.
source: Moreover, the rapid disassembly of spWsp1 and spMyo1 from endocytic sites supports the notion that actin nucleation by the two NPFs rapidly decreases while the invagination elongates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dynamics data presented in Figure 7.

claim: 92% (142 out of 154) of patches with assembled actin are non-motile during their lifetimes in the spwsp1-CA∆ mutant, indicating that endocytic internalization is strongly compromised.
source: Two-color live cell imaging demonstrated that the actin network (spFim1-mCherry) still assembles, but that 92% (142 out of 154) of patches with assembled actin are non-motile during their lifetimes, indicating that endocytic internalization is strongly compromised in the spwsp1-CA∆ mutant (Figure 8C and D, Video 1, and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color live-cell imaging data of the mutant presented in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Endocytic internalization still occurs in the spmyo1CA∆ mutant.
source: In contrast, endocytic internalization still occurs in the spmyo1CA∆ mutant (Figure 8E and F, Video 3, and Video 4), in which its 'CA' motif was precisely truncated at its genomic locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color live-cell imaging data of the mutant presented in Figure 8E and F.

claim: spWsp1 NPF activity is essential for endocytosis.
source: Together, these observations indicate that spWsp1 NPF activity is essential for endocytosis, that spMyo1 NPF activity is not, and they suggest that two-zone actin assembly is not required for endocytosis in fission yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic experiments with CA domain deletion mutants presented in Figure 8.

claim: spMyo1 NPF activity is not essential for endocytosis.
source: Together, these observations indicate that spWsp1 NPF activity is essential for endocytosis, that spMyo1 NPF activity is not, and they suggest that two-zone actin assembly is not required for endocytosis in fission yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic experiments with CA domain deletion mutants presented in Figure 8.

claim: Two-zone actin assembly is not required for endocytosis in fission yeast.
source: Together, these observations indicate that spWsp1 NPF activity is essential for endocytosis, that spMyo1 NPF activity is not, and they suggest that two-zone actin assembly is not required for endocytosis in fission yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic experiments with CA domain deletion mutants presented in Figure 8.

claim: The abundances of the endocytic protein homologues in the two yeasts are more similar than indicated by the published literature.
source: Strikingly, the abundances of the endocytic protein homologues in the two yeasts are more similar than indicated by the published literature (Figure 1, Figure 2A, Table 1, and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the side-by-side quantitative comparison data presented in Figures 1 and 2A, and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Each nanocage contains 120 copies of sfGFP.
source: We calibrated our microscope using as a standard particle a hyperstable, water-soluble 60-subunit protein nanocage (~25 nm diameter) with in-frame fusions of sfGFP (super-folder Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP)) to both termini of each subunit, so each particle contains 120 copies of sfGFP (Hsia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the nanocage standard supported by citation to the source.

claim: The mean fluorescence intensity of 120-sfGFP-tagged nanocages was linearly proportional to exposure time over a range from 100 ms to at least 1600 ms per frame.
source: The mean fluorescence intensity was linearly proportional to exposure time over a range from 100 ms to at least 1600 ms per frame (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calibration data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The numbers of endocytic proteins at endocytic sites in these two yeasts are much more similar than was previously thought.
source: In total, our direct, side-by-side comparison indicates that the numbers of proteins at endocytic sites in these two yeasts are much more similar than was previously thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative comparison data presented throughout the Results section.

claim: The modest differences between the two yeasts may help explain the differences in the dynamics.
source: The modest differences between the two yeasts may help explain the differences in the dynamics reported in the following sections.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the protein number differences.

claim: The transition to irregular movement of scAbp1-GFP beyond ~125 nm from the origin likely represents endocytic vesicle release in budding yeast.
source: Considering the fluorescence and EM data that reflects on endocytic membrane morphology, we conclude that the transition to irregular movement of scAbp1-GFP beyond ~125 nm from the origin likely represents endocytic vesicle release in budding yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on combining live-cell imaging data with previous EM studies showing invagination depth.

claim: Previous EM studies suggested that in budding yeast the distance between the base and the tip of the invaginated endocytic membrane often reaches about ~100 nm in depth before vesicle scission occurs.
source: Previous EM studies suggested that in budding yeast the distance between the base and the tip of the invaginated endocytic membrane often reaches about ~100 nm in depth before vesicle scission occurs (Kukulski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous EM study.

claim: The data for budding yeast agree well with those of Picco et al. (2015), in which Rvs167 dynamics was used to predict the scission point.
source: Our data for budding yeast agree well with those of Picco et al. (2015), in which Rvs167 (budding yeast amphiphysin) dynamics was used to predict the scission point.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citation.

claim: The two yeasts spend similar time deforming the membrane prior to scission.
source: The results demonstrate that both yeast spend similar time deforming the membrane prior to scission.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative analysis of protein dynamics presented in Figures 3-5.

claim: The resulting endocytic invagination of fission yeast appears to be nearly twice as long as in budding yeast.
source: However, the resulting endocytic invagination of fission yeast appears to be nearly twice as long as in budding yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative analysis of protein dynamics and STORM imaging presented in Figures 3-6.

claim: The greater length of endocytic actin structures observed in fission yeast is consistent with the possibility that the invaginated membrane that it covers is deeper than in budding yeast.
source: Thus, the greater length of endocytic actin structures observed in fission yeast is consistent with the possibility that the invaginated membrane that it covers is deeper than in budding yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the STORM imaging data presented in Figure 6.

claim: 3D-STORM results support the conclusion that fission yeast endocytic invaginations are deeper than those observed in budding yeast.
source: Together, our 3D-STORM results support the conclusion that fission yeast endocytic invaginations are deeper than those observed in budding yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the STORM imaging data presented in Figure 6.

claim: More than 70% of GFP-Las17 patches showed dynamics similar to those observed for Las17-GFP.
source: More than 70% of GFP-Las17 patches showed dynamics similar to those observed for Las17-GFP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data comparing N-terminal and C-terminal GFP fusions presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The populations of actin patches in the GFP-LAS17 strain and the LAS17-GFP strain were indistinguishable by patch lifetimes and actin network marker behavior.
source: In spite of these differences, the populations of actin patches in the GFP-LAS17 strain and the LAS17-GFP strain were indistinguishable by two criteria: (1) patch lifetimes were identical; and (2) the actin network markers Abp1p-RFP and Myo5p-RFP behaved similarly over space and time in the two strains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) (Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of patch dynamics in the two strains presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The differences between WASp dynamics in the two yeasts are real rather than resulting from differences in the fluorescent fusion proteins or differences in the analytical methods.
source: These observations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7A) confirm that the differences between WASp dynamics in the two yeasts are real rather than resulting from differences in the fluorescent fusion proteins or differences in the analytical methods.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of N-terminal and C-terminal GFP fusions and the dynamics data.

claim: spFim1 dynamics appear to be identical in spfim1-mEGFP, mEGFP-spwsp1 spfim1-mCherry, and mEGFP-spmyo1 spfim1-mCherry strains.
source: spFim1 dynamics appear to be identical in spfim1-mEGFP, mEGFP-spwsp1 spfim1-mCherry, and mEGFP-spmyo1 spfim1-mCherry strains (Figure 3G, Figure 7C and E), indicating that mEGFP fusions do not affect spWsp1's or spMyo1's function or actin patch dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of dynamics data across different strains presented in Figures 3G, 7C, and 7E.

claim: Vesicle scission appears to occur when actin assembly reaches its maximum level.
source: Consistently, vesicle scission appears to occur when actin assembly reaches its maximum level (Figure 3G, Figure 5B and D, Figure 7C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between actin dynamics and predicted scission timing presented in multiple figures.

claim: spMyo1 accumulates at endocytic sites with similar timing to spWsp1, using spFim1 accumulation as a temporal alignment reference.
source: spMyo1 accumulates at endocytic sites with similar timing to spWsp1, using spFim1 accumulation as a temporal alignment reference (Figure 7D and E and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The spWsp1CA∆-GFP mutant protein accumulates and persists at endocytic sites nearly three times longer than the wild-type protein without the pronounced movement detectable in the wild type cells.
source: The spWsp1CA∆-GFP mutant protein accumulates and persists at endocytic sites nearly three times longer than the wild-type protein without the pronounced movement detectable in the wild type cells (Figure 7A, Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data of the mutant presented in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The lifetimes of Myo1CA∆-GFP and wild-type mEGFP-spMyo1 in patches are indistinguishable.
source: Moreover, the lifetimes of Myo1CA∆-GFP and wild-type mEGFP-spMyo1 in patches are indistinguishable (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of patch lifetimes presented in Figure 8B.

claim: Knowing how many of each type of protein is present at an endocytic site is crucial for developing a quantitative understanding of CME.
source: Knowing how many of each type of protein is present at an endocytic site is crucial for developing a quantitative understanding of CME.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of quantitative measurements for understanding mechanisms.

claim: The numbers determined for budding yeast were generally 1.5–3 times higher than previously reported.
source: The numbers we determined for budding yeast were generally 1.5–3 times higher than previously reported (Figure 2E, F and G) (Picco et al., 2015), while the numbers we determined for three key fission yeast proteins (spWsp1, spVrp1 and spMyo1) were 1.5–2 times lower than previously reported by Sirotkin et al. (Figure 2E, F and G) (Sirotkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's measurements with previous studies.

claim: The numbers determined for three key fission yeast proteins (spWsp1, spVrp1 and spMyo1) were 1.5–2 times lower than previously reported by Sirotkin et al.
